analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare providers from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts, 48 hours a week, or 12 hours straight.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of the 118th Congress with only 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would use Medicare's power over hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other providers to stop them from forcing nurses into mandatory overtime. Nurses could not be required to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, more than 12 consecutive hours, or the 10 hours right after finishing a 12-hour stretch. It would also protect nurses who complain about violations, require posted schedules and notice policies, and allow fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses who would no longer face mandatory overtime, mandatory 10-hour rests after long shifts, and new whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections. Patients also benefit, since the bill cites research linking nurse fatigue to medical errors [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits providers that take Medicare patients from requiring nurses to work more than a previously scheduled shift, 48 hours in a workweek, or 12 consecutive hours, or to work during the 10 hours after a 12-hour shift [S2][S3].
Protects nurses who refuse mandatory overtime or report violations from being fired, demoted, disciplined, or reported to state licensing boards in retaliation [S3].

Lets nurses file complaints with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, requires investigations, and allows civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with steeper penalties for repeat offenders [S2][S3].

Exempts only declared emergencies and disasters, and even then only after the provider shows it tried to fill staffing needs another way; a labor dispute or 'consistent understaffing' does not count as an emergency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, and other Medicare providers, who would need to hire more staff or limit scheduling instead of extending nurses' hours. Some of that staffing cost could flow to Medicare, insurers, and patients [S3].

drawbacks.text: The limits could leave hospitals short-handed during staff shortages, since the emergency exception excludes shortages caused by 'consistent understaffing' — a hospital with chronic vacancies would have to cover shifts through hiring or voluntary overtime, which can be costly and difficult [S3].

A hospital's compliance costs for hiring additional nursing staff could be passed on to Medicare, private insurers, and patients, and rural or safety-net hospitals operating on thin margins could feel the squeeze [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge that limits on work hours can create 'potential pitfalls of discontinuity in care' when handoffs between shifts increase, even as it concludes the safety benefits outweigh that risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: shorter, more predictable nurse shifts and fewer fatigue-driven errors, paid for through higher staffing costs at hospitals and other providers. The bill is narrowly drawn — voluntary overtime stays legal, emergencies get a genuine escape valve, and stronger state laws are untouched — so the design is reasonable. The unresolved question is cost: who funds the extra staffing, and whether fragile rural hospitals can absorb it. Those questions never got examined because the bill never received a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on March 5, 2024, joined by Sens. Butler, Van Hollen, and Fetterman [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance that same day — the only action recorded beyond introduction [S5].
The bill had 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the Finance Committee never scheduled a markup or vote, so it died at the end of the 118th Congress [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, home health agencies, and other Medicare providers are better off, since they avoid the staffing limits, reporting requirements, and fines the bill would have imposed. Nurses and patients gain nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Nurse Overtime and Patient Safety Act and led it as sole sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Laphonza Butler, Chris Van Hollen, and John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how most senators would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would cap mandatory overtime at Medicare-participating hospitals and psychiatric, outpatient, and critical access hospitals, forcing them to staff shifts through hiring or voluntary overtime instead of extending nurses' hours. The cost savings hospitals preserve by defeating it come at the expense of rested nurses and lower error rates [S2][S3].

Home health agencies, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, ambulatory surgical centers, and rehabilitation agencies would face the same overtime caps and documentation and notice requirements as hospitals [S2][S3].

Nurses would gain enforceable overtime limits, mandatory 10-hour rests after 12-hour shifts, and whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, enforceable through complaints to HHS and civil money penalties [S3].
